## Nothing to install

macOS needs no permission setup and no driver install. `AppleUSBACM` holds
the board's CDC (serial) interfaces, so `libusb` cannot open the whole device
exclusively — its Darwin backend tolerates that and still sends control
requests straight to the device's endpoint 0 (`dfu-util` programs the UNO R4
through the same path). Claiming the `UsbIo` interface itself is optional on
macOS; the driver does it by default anyway, for exclusivity between two
processes that might both try to use the board.

You still need to build `arduino-io` yourself: the Xcode command line tools
(`xcode-select --install`) and CMake 3.24 or newer, then the same build as
any other platform:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver.git
cd ArduinoDriver
cmake -B build -DARDUINODRIVER_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build --config Release
cmake --install build --config Release --prefix ~/.local
```

## High Speed link quality on the Portenta H7

::: {.callout-warning}
## Symptom: `LIBUSB_ERROR_IO` on a streaming Portenta H7

The Portenta H7 enumerates at USB High Speed (480 Mbit/s), and its bulk
streaming endpoint is only as reliable as that link. In some cases, plugged straight into a
Mac's USB-C port, streams die every few seconds at high stream rates,
with `bulk IN transfer failed: LIBUSB_ERROR_IO` — logged as `device not
responding` (`0xe00002ed`) with `LIBUSB_DEBUG=2` — and now and then the board
can stop answering control requests altogether until it is replugged.

**Fix:** If you experience that behavior,put a USB hub between the computer and
the board. A hub receives and retransmits every High Speed packet, turning one
marginal link into two short ones, and still runs at 480 Mbit/s. A USB 3 hub
works too, because the board attaches to the USB 2.0 hub built into it. Prefer a
short cable as well. 

:::

This is specific to the Portenta H7's High Speed link on macOS's USB-C ports;
it is not a general macOS limitation and has not been reported for the
Full Speed boards.

**On low rate experiments** (static and quasi static ones), reading analog pins in  polling mode up to few hundred Hz, the link is reliable enough to run the experiments without a hub, regardless the board and the operating system.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Fine for analysis, not the acquisition host

macOS needs nothing installed and streams reliably once the hub fix above is
in place, which makes it a good place to develop and run the Python or R
analysis code. For the acquisition itself, prefer a [Linux
host](host-linux.qmd) — the timing is more consistent, as explained in
[Setting up a bench](index.qmd#host-operating-system).
:::
